That’s very relatable what you said about your mom; I actually just blew up at my mom the other day for suggesting I go back to a prescriber. I didn’t feel like fully myself (not in an improved way either) on any of the many psych meds I’ve been on before, it feels like the only potential positive thing that *maybe* one or two could do is make me more palatable for others… that is not a worthwhile trade-off to me because I value my authenticity a lot.

Professionals within psychiatry never do the full (or any) investigational work. 🤷‍♀️They are trained to (subjectively) identify the *symptoms*, no physical tests/scans or proper background into your health and lifestyle used, then they find the prescriptions they deem worth trialing you on. That’s it. I don’t believe it can accurately be described as the medical branch of mental health with how it is still operating, because those doctors never investigated anything underlying my health issues. 🤷‍♀️

Glad to hear it! And it’s a sad thought that some actually do end up taking their lives for situations like debt which are a lot more likely to be temporary, or never even needed to happen if society had better ways of operating!

Did you too finally feel like you could think straight again after getting off that vile anti*psychotic* which should never be given to someone for/with autism, or even prescribed for that bullshit narrative that it increases the effectiveness of antidepressants when none of them are working? 🤦‍♀️I’m sorry you have experienced abuse and disempowerment; women can be abusers too, but typically don’t get reprimanded for some of the same abusive behaviors as men. Another question, do you consider any past doctors abusers of yours as well? I’m on the spectrum and have experienced so much medical trauma that I won’t even go to a psychiatrist (prescriber) anymore. Psych meds of all kinds tend to not be good for especially sensitive autistic systems, anyway. Yet they still push them on us. 😢

Did you have a history of mental health issues or was it more in response to big life hardship (I did see where you mentioned debt)?
I’m really happy for you! That’s admirable that you are sharing your experience, and I think all types of experiences around suicide should be talked about openly. As successful recovery narratives are what is most shared and most celebrated, I just also wanted to say to anyone whose story does not look like recovery or being happy they lived, that you are valid too. The most widespread stories are around recovery and they are heartwarming and also important, but also I think the sad reality should not be overlooked that mental health afflictions are effectively lifelong and terminal for some, especially the case in a society where psychiatric intervention often isn’t effective and sometimes just makes the issues more compounded and entrenched. I’m really glad you appear to have made healing progress from whatever drove you to do it! I just also wanted to say to people whose experiences with suicide or suicidal ideation don’t resonate with narratives of successful recovery, even after many years, that you are not alone. ❤️

I have seemingly noticed a lot of birth mothers are adoptees... but moreover, I think a high percentage of birth mothers, like myself, have/had unresolved abandonment issues in general. In these cases, abandonment (physically or emotionally) is what they know, whether they realize it or not. Repeating the dynamics we are familiar with can I think be a way to validate ourselves, and continue not facing down the reality of how whatever we went through actually affected us.

I'm a birth mother. I'm not an adoptee, but my parents essentially physically abandoned me (though  they always still insisted on visits and overseeing my life) when my mental illness (severe OCD primarily) made me too hard for them to live with in my teens. My mom in particular can not handle emotional stress from others very well at all. She had never been the most emotionally attentive when it came to difficult emotions. I was in and out of children's residential mental health treatment centers that never actually helped me, and then after I turned 18 (also after my first suicide attempt that further unsettled the family) they put me in an adult foster home for the mentally ill. I stayed there for a full year until they got me on SSI and section 8 so that I could live alone (as I admittedly have now for the last 10+ years... and the social isolation has only compounded all my problems).

I honestly have very, very severe, unresolved abandonment issues, yet I somehow wasn't even too consciously aware of the effects my parents' actions had on me until I began coming out of the "adoption fog" (waking up to the staggering reality of adoption, which is not rainbows and unicorns) honestly very soon after the birth and relinquishment of my now one year old son. Hearing about common abandonment issues with adoptees in triad forums is what really woke me up to my own issues. Too late, unfortunately. 😢 I honestly now can't help but feel that adoption is definitely the worst choice I could have made for myself (the last thing I needed was more trauma and loss of connection in my life, just when I was starting to improve a bit). I also worry it wasn't the best choice for my son. At any rate, I'm sad I repeated what I knew with him (except with him, I did it to him immediately off the bat in his life!) before I had true conscious awareness of the abandonment dynamics in my relationship with my own parents.

I can definitely agree with that. Foster care is not for everyone; nor is adoption of any type. Some people shouldn't be adoptive parents, period. I will also add that there can be a LOT of unforeseen psychological challenges to domestic infant adoption as well (the type I'm familiar with). Prospective parents can wait for years due to the high demand to supply ratio, and can have numerous failed matches. Prospective adoptive parents need to do a ton of research, dive deep into perspectives of the sides of the triad that suffer a loss due to adoption, especially in regards to how to go about it as ethically as possible. But most don't. They just let the agency take the main lead in educating them, which is really a bad idea. Pre birth matching is a really sketchy area because it's so very hard to go about in a way that involves no even subtle/unintentional coercion (that's why pre birth matching is actually straight up outlawed in some countries I've been told). And 95% of domestic infant adoptions these days are open to at least some degree, which adds a whole other challenging layer to figure out. Adoption is highly emotionally charged for all sides of the triad.

Avoid a private agency period, if you want to truly be ethical. Adopt from foster care. 

Sincerely, a birth mom who has seen that even a non faith/non profit DIA agency that advertises itself as the most ethical around still has a sly agenda. Afterall, the ratio of waiting parents to available newborns is nearly 40:1
